The Treasure Island Waterfront Event Venue is the home of Soothe Our Souls , a nonprofit organization founded in 2012 by Captain Dan Peretz. This unique space offers the best of old-time Florida on a secluded piece of waterfront property with easy access to the Gulf of Mexico and Boca Ciega Bay. Located one block south of the famous John’s Pass Bridge on Treasure Island, the building was constructed in 1930 and served as the Treasure Island Firehouse for many years before it became the Boca Ciega Sail and Power Squadron. Today, it houses the small group of volunteers who lead SOS. We are proud of our heartwarming organization and excited to share our memorable space with you. All rental proceeds support SOS, whose mission is to provide complimentary sailing for seriously health challenged people. So when you rent the Treasure Island Waterfront Event Venue for your special event, you also make a difference and help create the change you want to see in the world.

Bonfoey who had also designed the 1915 city hall downtown and the new Cuban Club at Palm Avenue and 14th street that was also being completed at the same time as the new Italian Club. This new Italian Club included a combination of Italian, Spanish and Greek architecture. A true architectural gem. The history shared below, Commemorating the Centennial of the Italian Club Building, includes excerpts from a historical account prepared by the Honorable E.J. Salcines, whose research and storytelling have helped preserve the remarkable legacy of Tampa’s Italian community. His complete presentation is featured in the YouTube video on this page, offering an even deeper look into the people, traditions, and defining moments that shaped L’Unione Italiana. For more than 130 years, the Italian Club of Tampa—L’Unione Italiana—has stood as a symbol of courage, community, and the Italian-American experience. Founded on April 4, 1894, the Club was created by Italian immigrants who came together to support one another, preserve their heritage, and build a better life in Tampa. What began as a mutual-aid society with 127 members grew into one of Tampa’s most important cultural institutions. Through periods of tremendous growth, economic hardship, war, and social change, the Italian Club has remained a place where families gather, traditions continue, and generations come together. ChIJN8sNCu_ywogRDA1M-xpXwyE.about: Palm Harbor is an unincorporated area within Pinellas County. Palm Harbor Parks and Recreation (PHPR) is a nonprofit organization that oversees some county properties. We, along with the Palm Harbor Library, are overseen by a volunteer board called the Palm Harbor Community Service Agency (PHCSA, pronounced Fix-sa). PHCSA was established in 1985 according to Pinellas County Ordinance 85-28, to provide library and recreation services to the Palm Harbor Community Services District residents, a municipal services taxing unit. The 0.5 mills ad valorem tax, voted on by the residents of Palm Harbor, is allocated to library and recreation services. Any additional funds needed to operate are raised independently by each entity. Our Beginnings – Palm Harbor Recreation League The organization of recreational activities in Palm Harbor began when a group of volunteers aimed to create safe playing environments for residents, similar to those found in neighboring cities. In 1980, these volunteers established the Palm Harbor Recreation League. By 1985, the league became an integral part of the Community Services Agency (PHCSA), providing guidance and direction for leisure services in Palm Harbor. Since then, Palm Harbor Recreation has managed several facilities within the Palm Harbor area. In 1999, the Senior Center opened and quickly became a valued gathering place for the community. ChIJgxpZ2Yc53YgRFbQv4oDi1s8.about: The mission of Bonnet Springs Park is to enrich our community through nature, culture, recreation, and education. Our Park serves to unify the city’s diverse population, offering public spaces that serve the needs of many by providing engaging and diverse opportunities in education and recreation to residents and visitors. Lakeland was built around its railyards, once the heart of Florida’s phosphate and agricultural industries. For nearly a century, the city’s largest railyard connected communities, cities, and states until its closure in the early 1980s. What remained was 168 acres of neglected land, a forgotten chapter in Lakeland’s history. Remediation efforts began in 2019 to restore the land from the environmental impacts of past rail operations. Through the vision of community leaders and the expertise of world-renowned design firm Sasaki, this historic site transformed into a vibrant urban oasis. Today, Bonnet Springs Park stands as a testament to renewal, offering natural beauty, innovative spaces, and endless opportunities to Escape. Engage. Explore.

Historically, membership included hospital benefits, cemetery benefits and health insurance. The purpose of the club was to take care of its members from cradle to grave. ChIJo-8jH13EwogRuKIb6MNc2aA.about: In the late 1880s the immigrants who came to the Americas from Spain were largely bachelors or, if married came unaccompanied and sent for their families after earning sufficient funds for their passage. Consequently, there were a large number of Spaniards who had no one to care for them if they became ill or unable to work. Cuba was a Spanish possession until 1898 and Havana was the destination for many immigrants from Asturias, a province in northern Spain on the Bay of Biscay. In Havana, there existed organizations representing other regions in Spain such as Galicia, Cataluña and Castilla. On May 2, 1886, Centro Asturiano de La Habana was formed to provide medical assistance for the collective benefit of its members. Immigration from Cuba was not as restricted as it was from Europe. When the cigar industry came to Ybor City, there was a wave of immigration from Havana, where many had been employed in cigar manufacturing. In 1902, a group of 546 immigrants from the province of Asturias founded the Centro Asturiano de Tampa, one of the city's first mutual aid societies and a branch of the original club established in Havana, Cuba. Centro Asturiano began in a two-room, wood-frame building on Seventh Avenue. Membership rapidly grew and the club moved to an impressive new building at the corner of Palm and Nebraska. GFWC is one of the largest non-denominational wom e n’s organizations in the world with a motto of Unity in Diversity. This motto is embodied in the organization’s emblem. GFWC’s emblem depicts a circular band signifying eternity. In the center of the circular band, the crusader’s shield emerges from a darkened world (represented by the field of darkness), which represents enlightenment. The enameled colors—red, white, and blue—are the colors of the United States of America. The red implies courage, the white equals purity, and the blue stands for constancy. The GFWC Tampa Woman’s Club was organized in 1900 by 10 members as a cultural and social organization meeting regularly for literary discussions and refreshments at what is now the University of Tampa. As membership grew, their interests widened and in 1913 the Club was accepted into the GFWC Florida Federation of Wom e n’s Clubs (GFWC Florida). Educational and welfare projects became part of the members’ concerns. St. Petersburg has always been characterized by endless sunshine, soaring pelicans, and a glistening waterfront, so it’s easy to imagine what attracted its founders here nearly 150 years ago. Like most of the United States, the Tampa Bay area was home to generations of Indigenous tribes before the first White settlers arrived. While Spanish explorers came and went in the 1500s, it wasn’t until much later that the St. Pete we know began to form. People began moving to the area during the 1830s and 1840s, setting up homesteads, planting citrus and other crops, and raising animals. After the Civil War, more settlers arrived, including the area's first Black settlers, John Donaldson and Anna Germain , in 1868. In 1875 John Constantine Williams of Detroit, Michigan moved to Tampa and bought 2,500 acres of warm waterfront land that would eventually become St. Petersburg. Thirteen years later, he transferred part of that land to Peter Demens, an exiled Russian aristocrat. In exchange, Demens extended the Orange Belt Railroad to Williams’s settlement. The University’s intent is not to prescribe, but to aid students in developing a sense of purpose and self-awareness through reflection and learning to make decisions based on principles, beliefs and values. It is UTampa’s goal to become a model of understanding and cooperation. Through work with the Interfaith Youth Core , a Chicago-based international leader in interfaith cooperation, the University is building the framework for a sustainable interfaith leadership program. This partnership puts the University at the forefront of a White House initiative called the President’s Interfaith and Community Service Campus Challenge that asks university presidents to commit to promoting interfaith cooperation and community service on their campuses.
